messages.body_plain:
Does the following code match your survey design?  (I'm assuming there are no site or visit covariates.)

# Estimation with a mixture of 1-visit and multi-visit sites

# Set some parameters to generate some data
  psi = 0.6  # Probability of presence
  p = 0.4    # Detection probability
  v = 5      # Number of visits
  n1 = 190    # Sites with 1 visit
  n = 10     # Sites with v visits

# Generate site status and detections
  status = rbinom(n1+n,1,psi)
  x = status*matrix(rbinom(v*(n1+n),1,p),nrow=n1+n)
  x[1:n1,2:v] = NA
  x = unmarkedFrameOccu(x)

# Maximum likelihood estimates
  library(unmarked)
  y = occu(~1 ~1,x)
  summary(y)
  backTransform(y, type="det")
  backTransform(y, type="state")

Jim

messages.body_plain:
Hi Mikey,

I think "the program" is "doing" exactly what you say. I can't describe this in respectful algebra, but intuitively, you are absolutely right: you obtain information about detection probability solely from those sites surveyed multiple times and this estimate is applied to reduce uncertainty about the occupancy status of sites where the species was not detected among those that were only visited once.

This approach is valid under the important assumption that the sites with multiple visits are a random sample from the statistical population of sites for which you want to make an inference (i.e., estimate occupancy etc). If only the "better" sites, say, are visited multiple times, where by better I mean that they are those where you expected higher population densities and therefore higher likelihood of seeing the species, then this approach is not valid. In that you will overestimate detection probability (because the better sites have higher population density and therefore a greater probability that the species is seen) and therefore underestimate occupancy for the entire statistical population of sites.
o e
This is an interesting example of an "integrated analysis", where one may say you combine two types of data to get better precision and/or the ability to estimate additional parameters, in the spirit of "integrated population models" (Besbeas, Schaub etc...). Without the sample of sites visited multiple times, the data subset for the sites visited only once is useless to obtain an unbiased estimate of occupancy, but when you combine it with an information-richer sample that contains info about p, you can exploit the info in both sources of info.

There are many possibilties in population analysis to combine data sets of multiple types. This is being increasingly done in statistical ecology. Other examples are the approach of Conroy et al (Ecology, ~2008), where they combine cheap occupancy data over an extensive area with expensive cap-recap data to estimate abundance over the wider area, or the approach of Miller et al. (Ecology, ~2011) to combine two types of data quality in an occupancy model to estimate both false-negative and false-positive errors. And many more !

Kind regards  --  Marc

# ... So that I have one 'fm' for each possible combination of the effects of each covariate on   both detection probability and occupancy.

messages.body_plain:
I’d like to argue that the sites with just a single visit do contribute to the estimation of the detection probability.  (And I’m also simplifying the example by having no covariates.)

The argument is that if one keeps the same histories for the multi-visit sites but removes some of the single-visit histories, the maximum likelihood estimate of the detection probability does change.  Below is an example with the structure that Mikey used:

# Estimation with a mixture of 1-visit and multi-visit sites

# Set some parameters to generate some data

  psi = 0.6  # Probability of presence

  p = 0.4    # Detection probability

  v = 5      # Number of visits

  n1 = 190   # Sites with 1 visit

  n = 10     # Sites with v visits

# Generate site status and detections

  status = rbinom(n1+n,1,psi)

  logArea = rnorm(n1+n)

  x = status*matrix(rbinom(v*(n1+n),1,p), nrow = n1 + n)

  x[1:n1, 2:v] = NA

  x.ufo = unmarkedFrameOccu(x)

# Maximum likelihood estimates with original dataset

  library(unmarked)

  y = occu(~1 ~1, x.ufo)

  summary(y)

  backTransform(y, type="det")

  backTransform(y, type="state")

# Now remove the first half of the single visit sites

  nremove = floor(n1/2)

  x.remove = x[(n+n1-nremove):(n+n1),]

  xr.ufo = unmarkedFrameOccu(x.remove)

  yr = occu(~1 ~1, xr.ufo)

  summary(yr)

  backTransform(yr, type="det")

  backTransform(yr, type="state")

The difference will usually not be very much but both parameters (detection probability and probability of presence) are estimated simultaneously with all of the data.

Jim

Hi Mikey,

I think that my reply was a bit more general than your question. I don’t think that you should describe your approach in this generality. Actually, I think that in many published occupancy studies some sites will have only one visits. One I know this for sure is this:

Kéry, M., Gardner, B., & Monnerat, C. 2010. Predicting species distributions from checklist data using site-occupancy models. Journal of Biogeography 37: 1851–1862.

There, we had two thirds of the sites visited only once. The following was how we described what we did : „We surveyed individual sites 1–22 (mean 1.8) times per year, with 937 (32%) surveyed more than once in a single season. By repeatedly visiting sites, we obtained the data necessary to estimate the detection probability in the site-occupancy model.“

Kind regards  ---  Marc

I’d like to argue that the sites with just a single visit do contribute to the estimation of the detection probability.  (And I’m also simplifying the example by having no covariates.)

The argument is that if one keeps the same histories for the multi-visit sites but removes some of the single-visit histories, the maximum likelihood estimate of the detection probability does change.  Below is an example with the structure that Mikey used:

# Estimation with a mixture of 1-visit and multi-visit sites

# Set some parameters to generate some data

  psi = 0.6  # Probability of presence

  p = 0.4    # Detection probability

  v = 5      # Number of visits

  n1 = 190   # Sites with 1 visit

  n = 10     # Sites with v visits

# Generate site status and detections

  status = rbinom(n1+n,1,psi)

  logArea = rnorm(n1+n)

  x = status*matrix(rbinom(v*(n1+n),1,p), nrow = n1 + n)

  x[1:n1, 2:v] = NA

  x.ufo = unmarkedFrameOccu(x)

# Maximum likelihood estimates with original dataset

  library(unmarked)

  y = occu(~1 ~1, x.ufo)

  summary(y)

  backTransform(y, type="det")

  backTransform(y, type="state")

# Now remove the first half of the single visit sites

  nremove = floor(n1/2)

  x.remove = x[(n+n1-nremove):(n+n1),]

  xr.ufo = unmarkedFrameOccu(x.remove)

  yr = occu(~1 ~1, xr.ufo)

  summary(yr)

  backTransform(yr, type="det")

  backTransform(yr, type="state")

The difference will usually not be very much but both parameters (detection probability and probability of presence) are estimated simultaneously with all of the data.

Jim

The link below contains Stan code for a working occupancy model and a suggestion from Bob Carpenter (a Stan developer) that it will be incorporated into an ecology portion of the manual.  He also references work on a Cormac-Jolly-Seber model in Stan.

https://groups.google.com/d/topic/stan-users/EpX-wzOj7L4/discussion

The problem is that discrete random variables need to be marginalized out to calculate the gradient of the log probability function.  The Stan manual has a chapter devoted to Mixture Modeling where it discusses approaches to fit, for example, zero-inflated models.  The whole advantage of Hamiltonian Monte Carlo is the speed and convergence improvements of calculating that gradient.  But as pointed out in the discussion above, it seems like marginalizing out discrete parameters defeats the purpose of Bayesian estimation.

I suppose the details ultimately don't matter if the workaround still improves estimation metrics compared to BUGS models.  But it appears that this MCMC sampler is fundamentally not designed to handle discrete random variables.

Dear Auriel,

it seems to me that you don't provide the starting values in the proper format. You need to provide starting values for every parameter in your model and, of course, in the right order. Your global model has something like 17 params, so your inits must be an expression "c(...)" with 17 elements. Use the solutions from another, similar, "neighbouring" model as starting values for the global model. If that model has fewer params then "fill in" the remaining inits with 0.

Perhaps as an illustration, here's some code where I did this for a model fit with gdistsamp. I used the solutions from a smaller model fm3M (with 2 fewer parameters) as starting values for the larger model (fm4MA).

Kind regards  --  Marc

starts <- c(tmp$lambda@estimates, tmp$phi@estimates, tmp$det@estimates, 0,0, tmp$scale@estimates)

# Fit model with these inits

   phiformula = ~(rep-1)+ POTATO+GRASS+LSCALE,

   pformula = ~DATE + HOUR,

Hi Auriel,
   I can never remember what the correct order for the starting values is, but you can use "coef(MODELNAME)" to make sure you have them in the correct order. Often, I will first run a model using the poisson mixture, as they tend to converge better, and then use those parameter estimates as starts when I try the NB mixture. That code looks like this, with the important part in bold:

HZ_Null_P<-gdistsamp(~1,~1,~1,keyfun="hazard", unitsOut="ha", mixture="P", output="density",data=umf)
HZ_Null_NB<-gdistsamp(~1,~1,~1,keyfun="hazard", unitsOut="ha",mixture="NB", output="density",data=umf,
starts=c(as.numeric(coef(HZ_Null_P)),0))
Basically, it pulls the coefficients from the poisson model and then adds a starting value of 0 for the dispersion parameter.

Hope this helps!

Andrew

We completely agree about the single-visit sites contributing to the occupancy estimate only when the detection estimate comes from elsewhere.  (Otherwise, of course, we can only estimate the product of occupancy and the detection probability.)

However, I still want to make the case that adding single-visit sites changes the maximum likelihood estimate of the detection probability (sometimes drastically) and the maximum likelihood estimate of occupancy.  Further, depending on the underlying detection probability and occupancy probability, adding single-visit sites can make things worse or have a minimal improvement.

Consider as in Mikey's example of 10 sites with 5 visits and we set p = 0.2, and psi = 0.2.  With 190 added single-visit sites the root mean square error for the mle of p is around 0.1724.  If we only added 10 single-visit sites, the rmse is around 0.0815:  roughly half of what we get from 190 single-visit sites.  The rmse for the mle of psi drops from 0.2161 with 10 single-visit sites to 0.1803 with 190 single-visit sites.  In this case there does not seem to be much of any advantage to add single-vist sites.  Below is a table of these results:

10 5-visit sites
detection probability = 0.2
occupancy probability = 0.2

Results for adding 10 and 190 single-visit sites
p-hat:                     Mean     Std. Err.     RMSE
   190 1-visit sites:      0.3594     0.3688     0.1614
    10 1-visit sites:      0.2134     0.2688     0.0724

psi-hat:                   Mean     Std. Err.     RMSE
   190 1-visit sites:      0.4166     0.3954     0.2032
    10 1-visit sites:      0.4602     0.4104     0.2361

When the occupancy and detection probabilities are larger there can be an advantage to having single visit sites.  But maybe not as large as might be desired.

Below is the R code I used for generating the above summary statistics using unmarked.  (The example runs for about 90 seconds on my laptop.)

# Maximum likelihood estimation with a mixture of 1-visit and multi-visit sites
# Load library
  library(unmarked)

# Define function to produce simulations
  mle.psi.p <- function(n1, n, v, nsim , psi, p) {

# Initialize vectors holding maximum likelihood estimates
  p.hat <- NULL
  psi.hat <- NULL

# Perform simulations and find parameter estimates
  for (i in 1:nsim) {

      # Generate simulated data
      status <- rbinom(n1+nv,1,psi)
      x <- status*matrix(rbinom(v*(n1+nv),1,p),nrow=n1+nv)
      x[1:n1,2:v] <- NA
      x <- unmarkedFrameOccu(x)

      # Maximum likelihood estimates
      y <- occu(~1 ~1,x)
      p.hat[i] <- backTransform(y, type="det")@estimate
      psi.hat[i] <- backTransform(y, type="state")@estimate
  }
  p.mean <- mean(p.hat)
  p.se <http://p.se> <- sd(p.hat)
  p.rmse <- (p.mean-p)^2 + p.se <http://p.se>^2
  psi.mean <- mean(psi.hat)
  psi.se <http://psi.se> <- sd(psi.hat)
  psi.rmse <- (psi.mean-psi)^2 + psi.se <http://psi.se>^2

  return(list(n1,nv,v,p.mean,p.se <http://p.se>,p.rmse,psi.mean,psi.se <http://psi.se>,psi.rmse))
}
# Set some values for parameters
  psi <- 0.2   # Probability of presence
  p <- 0.2     # Detection probability
  v <- 5       # Number of visits to multi-visit sites
  nv <- 10     # Number of sites with v visits
  nsim <- 1000 # Number of simulations

# 190 1-visit sites
  sim190 <- mle.psi.p(190, nv, v, nsim, psi, p)

# 10 1-visit sites
  sim10 <- mle.psi.p(10, nv, v, nsim, psi, p)

# Comparison
  cat("p-hat:                     Mean     Std. Err.     RMSE\n",
   "  190 1-visit sites: ",sprintf("%10.4f",c(sim190[[4]],sim190[[5]],sim190[[6]])),"\n",
   "   10 1-visit sites: ",sprintf("%10.4f",c(sim10[[4]], sim10[[5]], sim10[[6]])), "\n")
  cat("psi-hat:                   Mean     Std. Err.     RMSE\n",
   "  190 1-visit sites: ",sprintf("%10.4f",c(sim190[[7]],sim190[[8]],sim190[[9]])),"\n",
   "   10 1-visit sites: ",sprintf("%10.4f",c(sim10[[7]], sim10[[8]], sim10[[9]])), "\n")

Jim, I'm not sure you should read too much into those low-data scenarios.  These models will perform very poorly when the replication is low and the true probabilities are also low.  FWIW, I could not get your simulation to work with 10 single-visit sites at the values you provided.  Anybody that is trying to estimate a low detection probability with only 10 sites and 5 visits is going to have trouble.  As your results indicated, neither scenario could really identify the true values and both had huge SEs for the estimates.

If you change the probabilities from 0.2 to 0.35 (for both occupancy and detection), you'll find the results make more sense.  Alternatively, if you have more replication for the multi-visit sites (e.g., nv = 50) and keep the low probabilities then the results also improve and there is little distinction between estimates for 10 vs 190 single visits.  And in these "more data" scenarios, the additional single-visit sites always improve the SEs.

This definitely underscores the importance of simulation, which Marc has certainly been vocal about.

The code was correct, as far as I can tell, but the 10 single-visit scenario leads me to a singular Hessian.  I tried some different starting values (including the true ones) and that did not help.  But this is besides the point.

I agree with you that single visits do influence the likelihood for both occupancy and detection probabilities, but I contend that the influence on detection is only significant under poor data scenarios where the information content is very low.  If you have reasonable replication for a portion of sites so that the estimation of detection is adequate, the single visits no longer influence the detection likelihood significantly.

Without any secondary replication, if you visit 10 sites and detect the species at 5 of them, the range of plausible parameter values for both occupancy and detection is 0.50-1.00.  Either half the sites are occupied and your detection is perfect, or all the sites are occupied and a detection occurs half the time (or anything in between, of course).  The fact that the data do not support values <0.50 for either probability represents information in the likelihood.  When you actually do have replication in a second dimension, your ability to separate the mixture is drastically improved.  But that replication has to provide enough information to allow adequate estimation of the mixture.  With 5 visits and p=0.2, your probability of detecting a species is 0.67 across all visits.  With only 10 sites and psi=0.2, that means your detection information is potentially coming from only 1-2 sites.  The information content in that scenario is so low that the additional information from 190 single-visit sites is enough to influence the likelihood.

So the bottom line for me is that single-visit sites are only a concern, in terms of the influence on detection probability, when the information content of your sites with secondary replication is low enough that you shouldn't be using a formal mixture model in the first place.  The information content is proportional to your total detections, determined by the amounts of primary and secondary replication and the probabilities of occupancy and detection.

Dear Jim, and hello Dan,

OK, you convinced me that single visits do contain info also about detection probability. However, without having at least some sites with multiple visits, one cannot extract this information. This is similar to integrated population models, where a time series of counts also contains info about survival rates (because any change in N at that site must be due to B-I-D-E), but without extra information such as ring-recovery data (or strong priors in a Bayesian analysis), you cannot extract this info from the counts alone.

Re. any doubts about whether to include or not any single-visit data, I would feel that you should, but only if the single-visit sites are a sample from the same population of sites as are the sites with more than one visit.
